Corona virus and the economy

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
...how is and how will the Corona virus impact the world and the South African economy

Unique Selling Point:
Current affairs -- different take on the Coronavirus pandemic

Summary:
The measures implemented to contain the virus is having a massive effect on the world economy. These measures include the shutting of factories, quarantining people, limiting travel and movement and so on. It has an incredibly widespread knock-on effect that is affecting and will affect South Africa's day to day living and individual finances fundamentally. In this insert, we investigate the effect of the virus on the economy and people's everyday lives.

Further information:
The measures implemented to contain the virus is having a massive effect on the world economy. These measures include the shutting of factories, quarantining people, limiting travel and movement and so on. It has an incredibly widespread knock-on effect that is affecting and will affect South Africa's day to day living and individual finances fundamentally. In this insert, we investigate the effect of the virus on the economy and people's everyday lives.

In the story, we will look at the impact on the financial markets, the world economy and the South African economy, that is, macro-economic factors. We will look at the "supply shock" and the "demand shock" of the pandemic and how each will impact on economies and people's lives.

However, we will also take a look at how it is impacting and will impact the real economy -- ordinary people's everyday lives. Here we will use a fictional example of a single mother and her child as an example to illustrate the current and potential impact on people's lives -- from personal finances to ordinary medicine and holidays.

There are reports that i-Phones are in short supply and that people have begun to stockpile. We will see if we can get footage of this as well.

Interviewees:
Dawie Roodt, Chief Economist, Efficient Group (Monday 9 March 15:30)
Prof. Uma Kollamparambil, Head of the Economics Department, Wits (Wednesday 11 March, 08:00)
Elize Kruger, Independent Economist (Thursday 10:00)


Also looking into the possibility of interviewing somebody who is currently in a quarantined city

Press Release:


Counting the Costs of COVID-19
Now declared a global pandemic, the coronavirus is having a major impact on international financial markets. Uncertainty and fear of a worldwide recession sent stock markets spiraling down to new record lows. In South Africa, a trillion Rands in value was effectively wiped off the Johannesburg Stock Exchange in a single day, while US stocks fell 7% on Tuesday this week, forcing the US government to announce new economic measures to shore up the economy and lessen the impact of the virus. In Europe the Bank of England and the European Central Bank have both slashed interest rates in a in a desperate move to protect the UK and EU member states from the potentially catastrophic effect of COVID-19.
Producer: Eugene Botha | Presenter: Derek Watts


Script:


V/O:
Covid-19 is rapidly changing the world as we know it – and not for the better.
6000 people have died,
More than a 100 million people have been placed in total lockdown.
Major sporting events are being cancelled all over the world.
Donald Trump has announced a travel ban, preventing people from Europe from travelling to the US.
What was termed an Outbreak is now officially recognized as a pandemic.

World financial markets are crashing, wiping trillions of rand off the value of stocks and shares and pushing the world towards a global recession.

But while we in South Africa have so far been spared the worst in terms of deaths and number of infections, we have not escaped the financial meltdown.
LINK:
The economic impact of the corona virus on the South African economy the last two weeks has been most visible here, at the JSE.
V/O:
Elize Kruger is an independent economist and is following developments on the financial markets closely.
Elize:
So last week we saw the largest drop in the JSE in about 20 years following what is happening overseas.
V/O:
On that one day the JSE lost one trillion rand of its value. And despite news from China that infection rates are slowing down and people are returning to work, the bloodbath on world markets continued this week.
Elize:
Markets have plummeted in SA following global markets that are reacting on the spreading of the coronavirus. The JSE has shed about 20% of the market since the beginning of the year, of which the majority was in the past 2 weeks.
V/O:
Economist Dawie Rood says we must put blame for what is happening where it belongs.
Dawie:
I think it is important to realise that the virus itself is not causing all this damage. The real damage has been done by the measures that have been put into place to contain the virus. For example, if you close a city simply isolate a city, it will impact the city’s GDP or economic activity. That is where the real damage is
V/O:
Containment measures include restricting the movement of individuals, closing of factories, air travel bans and confining people to their homes. All of this has economic ramifications.
LINK:
The world and local economies are basically affected in two ways by something like a pandemic. Economists talk about a “supply shock”.
Dawie:
Dawie: We have already seen that certain factories are closed down. Because they are scared of the virus, or people have been sent home. And that means there is a supply shock, stuff is simply not being manufactured. A good example is that SA want’s to import certain stuff from China, and we can’t get that because the factories are simply closed.
V/O:
Prof Uma Kollamparambil of Wits University says even the unavailability of a single product can affect supply chains worldwide.

Uma:
The world is such an integrated place now. For example, we can’t pride ourselves to be producing the BMW car ourselves in SA at least. But understand, what we are doing is only assembling it. Now the BMW car involves about 12000 suppliers from 70 countries. Now if there is a shutdown in any one of these countries, and the essential parts for the manufacture of this care does not reach SA, for all purposes, production cannot carry on. So, it is an intricate network between the production line and across countries, which has put at risk the entire world economy.
V/O:
The stringent control measures to contain the virus also cause a demand shock that can affect economies significantly.
Uma:
Prof Uma: Demand shock is when the consumer either does not have capacity to generate demand, in other words just does not have the purchasing power. Or, has the purchasing power, but now needs to procrastinate that decision, because of uncertainties of the future.
Dawie:
A good example is people are just not going overseas anymore, they’re not buying overseas trips anymore, they are not buying vacations anymore. And that is a demand shock, so we see a shock on both sides of the economy.
V/O:
These two factors result in a massive slowdown of world trade and, linked to sustained uncertainty about the outcome of the pandemic, have a devastating effect on economies. This past week Central Banks and Governments have announced a series of measures to counter the economic slowdown. They announced the lowering of interest rates and massive stimulus packages. So far, it has had little effect. The world economy is in tatters.
Elize:
Unless we see some certainty coming to the markets, and that will probably have to come from something like the development of the vaccine and so, we could potentially see that this would move towards a global recession environment.
V/O:
This will cause high unemployment, falling incomes, reduced economic activity and increased poverty. It will also have a detrimental effect on pension funds.

One of the worst hit countries in the world is Italy which is now in a total lockdown.

Lisa Bergami is a South African in living there.
LISA:
Everything is closed, so basically now our shops are closed, restaurants are closed, bars are closed, ja, this town is like a ghost town. You’re not allowed to travel in and out. You need to have a special pass with you, if it’s work-related, or if you have a medical emergency. But you can’t leave the house. There’s a restaurant downstairs from where I live and the other day, I spoke to the manager there, I said so you closed completely? And he said there is no point in staying open during the day, this was before the big lockdown, there was no point in staying open during the day because people were too scared to sit next to each other. So, then I think to myself well how’s he going to earn his money you know? There are no commercial activities going on, except for a pharmacy, pharmacies are allowed to stay open, and supermarkets. It is tough and it is depressing, I think it is human nature that people want to be in contact with other people you know. You want to talk, you want to have a conversation, you want to grab a cup of coffee. I don’t think the population in Italy was aware, neither was I, that this virus will take over, and so quickly.
V/O:
We also managed to Skype with South African Kathy Grant who lives in Padua in Northern Italy.
Kathleen section



V/O:
Could South Africa also be heading towards a total lockdown? Will our towns also become ghost towns such as those in Italy? Nobody really knows. However, we are clearly beginning to see the impact of the pandemic on tourism and in the availability of certain goods such as electronics and iPhones.
Uma:
The impact that we’ve witnessed so far, like I said it is only next to the global financial crisis. But it has the potential to blow up even bigger and come out as a catastrophic event in history. Which can change global dynamics.
LINK:
As terrible and unsure as the situation is today, a massive global economic crisis is perhaps not without some positive outcomes.
V/O:
In times of uncertainty investors turn to gold and the price has risen considerably over the last few days. This could benefit our economy as South Africa is a major producer of gold.

Further, economists all say that the markets will eventually recover, as they always do, and that even a slow recovery will not be all that bad.
Uma:
If this prolongs this could result in checks and balances on the rise of China as a dominant power. And all the dependence of countries and the realisation of countries, that the risk involved and all the dependence on a single country, brought us export markets, as well as a source of imports.
Dawie:
Don’t see this as only bad. There are many positives to this as well.
V/O:
One of these is that the crisis is forcing individuals, governments, companies and educational institutions to utilize technology, and artificial Intelligence in new and innovative ways to cope with the challenges brought about by the pandemic.
Dawie:
We were gradually moving into the Fourth Industrial Revolution, in this new world of technology. The virus is simply accelerating the process.
